standard.title: Population Movements and Settlement Patterns 1750–1900
standard.description: the changing population movements and settlement patterns during the period 1750 to 1900
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe changes and continuities in earlier societies and identify causes of significant developments (AC9HH8K07, AC9HH8K12). They have not yet examined the specific mechanisms — agricultural enclosures, factory system, steam engine — that drove urbanisation and population redistribution in the modern period, or traced the multiple simultaneous movement patterns of this era.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the reasons for changing population movements in the period 1750–1900 — including agricultural change, industrialisation, and push factors from the slave trade, Irish Potato Famine and convict transportation — and describe how these movements changed settlement patterns.

nodes.label: Agricultural change and rural displacement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how changes to agricultural practices — enclosures, mechanisation — displaced rural populations and created pressure to move.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe enclosures as a practice of converting common land to private ownership, explain that mechanisation reduced demand for agricultural labour, and describe the resulting pressure on rural workers to move to cities or emigrate.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the enclosure movement and its effects on common land rights and subsistence farming; agricultural machinery (seed drill, threshing machines) and their labour displacement effects; the resulting rural unemployment and poverty; the movement of displaced agricultural workers into urban industrial centres; connect agricultural change to the Industrial Revolution context (K13).
wider: Examine the enclosure movement through the perspectives of both landowners (efficiency, profit) and displaced rural workers (loss of livelihood, traditional rights) — exploring how the same change was experienced very differently
Compare the British enclosure experience with agricultural change in other European contexts to assess whether Britain was typical or exceptional
nodes.hinge_reason: Agricultural displacement is the foundation for understanding urbanisation (N2) and the push factors for the slave trade and famine migrations (N3). Students who cannot explain rural displacement cannot explain why cities grew, why people sought factory work, or why emigration became attractive — the movement patterns in subsequent nodes all flow from this structural change.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat urbanisation as simply 'people moved to cities for jobs' without understanding the push mechanism — that agricultural change actively displaced rural populations. Making the displacement mechanism explicit is the scaffold for understanding N2 and N3.

success_criteria: Describes enclosures and mechanisation as causes of rural displacement
Explains how agricultural change created pressure on rural workers to move

nodes.label: Industrialisation and urbanisation — the factory system and city growth
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how the factory system and the development of the steam engine created demand for urban labour and drove the growth of industrial cities.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the factory system as concentrating production in cities, explain that steam power enabled factories and railways, and describe the resulting growth of industrial cities as workers moved to find employment.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the factory system as an organisational and technological shift from cottage industry; the role of steam in driving factories, mills and railways; how railways enabled movement of goods and people; the rapid growth of industrial cities (Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow); the conditions in industrial cities — overcrowding, poor sanitation, child labour; connect factory demand to the rural displacement from N1 as complementary push and pull.
wider: Examine the growth of a specific industrial city using census data or visual sources — tracking how population size, occupational structure and neighbourhood composition changed over decades
Investigate the role of railways in reshaping settlement patterns — not just connecting existing cities but enabling new towns to grow around railway junctions and industrial sites

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat urbanisation as a single undifferentiated movement rather than as two complementary forces — rural push and urban pull — operating together. Explicitly connecting N1 and N2 as push-pull mechanisms consolidates the causal framework.

success_criteria: Describes how the factory system and steam power concentrated production in cities
Explains how industrialisation created demand for urban labour and drove city growth

nodes.label: Forced and crisis-driven movements — slave trade, Irish Famine, convict transportation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the push factors driving three major forced or crisis-driven population movements of the period — the transatlantic slave trade, the Irish Potato Famine, and convict transportation — and describe the settlement patterns each produced.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe each of the three movements, identify the push factor(s) for each, and describe where affected populations moved to.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the transatlantic slave trade's scale, routes and nations involved (Portugal, Britain, France, Spain, North America); the Irish Potato Famine's causes, death toll and the destinations of emigration (USA, Canada, Australia); convict transportation — numbers, period, destinations (NSW, Van Diemen's Land); explain how each movement was driven by different combinations of forced removal and crisis; distinguish these from the voluntary urbanisation patterns in N1–N2; examine the long-term settlement patterns each created in receiving countries.
wider: Use data on the movement of peoples — slave trade statistics, famine emigration records, convict transportation records — to evaluate the relative scale of each movement and what the data reveals
Examine how the receiving countries — USA, Canada, Australia — were shaped by each of these movements, and how descendants of each group experience the legacy of those movements today
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Quantitative data analysis provides a genuinely different analytical lens from narrative description — examining scale through statistics builds historical evidence skills. The legacy question connects to contemporary relevance without departing from the Y9 content scope.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly focus on one of these movements (usually the one with the most classroom time) without understanding that the period was characterised by multiple simultaneous large-scale movements with different causes and mechanisms. Three distinct cases build the full picture the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Describes each of the three movements (slave trade, Irish Famine, convict transportation), identifies push factors, and describes destinations
Distinguishes forced/crisis-driven movement from voluntary urbanisation, explaining what makes each different
